Yes, this is a very good game, but it's not perfect. The gameplay becomes boring after a while, because you're always gathering the same items over and over again, some of which have no use for a long time (after 140  hours of play, I still don't know what to do with the Big Clams, the Dry Bricks or the silver underwater plant thingy). I suppose they will be useful at some point, but when, and how many of them will I need? I also don't like to see the water regularly inundating the building. It doesn't damage anything, but it's a terrible fail for the immersion. 
The acquisition of the recycler brings a new dimension to the game (trading), but it looks foreign to the game. As if it was added there only to break the monotony of the game. It doesn't feel like a logical feature of the game, like the sharks or the islands are.
And how the hell does the radar work? How do we use the radar to reach an island seen on it?

Bought Raft because I wanted a relaxing survival game where I could gather resources, explore, craft and slowly turn absolutely nothing into something. Think Stranded Deep, except your home comes along for the ride.

Six hours into my first evening, I was completely hooked. I even dreamt about the game that night.

My first run ended because I didn't notice the thirst bar. Surrounded by an entire ocean, I naturally tried drinking seawater. Didn't end well.

My second run ended when I crashed into an island without enough materials to craft a paddle, while a shark slowly ate my house. Lovely neighbourhood.

Third time's the charm, though. Every disaster teaches you something, every upgrade feels earned, and things that initially terrify you eventually become minor inconveniences. There's always something to gather, improve or explore, and the game happily lets you progress at your own pace.

The game could do a better job explaining the basics. I spent HOURS believing fishing required special bait because the interface kept suggesting I attach some. Instead of simply fishing to feed myself, I spent hours praying for an island or a floating crate that contained some potatoes.

If you love that explore, gather, return, craft, improve loop, this game is an absolute gem. One of those rare games where you sit down for an hour and somehow lose an entire weekend.

If you are here purely for a great gameplay experience with your friends, you may find yourself a little disappointed. Realistically, I'd say that Raft is a 5/10 game that I am a little hard-pressed to recommend to anyone. It feels cheaply cobbled together, with insane levels of jankiness and clipping, cut corners, lack of quality testing, and the most rudimentary gameplay loop under the sun. And yet, this game has some eldritch power that causes my friends and I to undergo major psychosis and delirium while playing. Its a really strange experience, and one that I love, even if the game is a little dubious in its make.

On an objective level, Raft is very poorly put together. Like, the main gameplay loop is just drifting through the water, sometimes completely directionless. You just collect materials to build the raft, as well as food and water to sustain yourself. The open sea might be a cool thematic choice, but it also allows the devs to starve you of any real content or landmarks. You'll run into generic islands, maybe some sunken rafts as well. But that's really about it for about 95% of the time. It's very barren, especially in a drought of resources where you just don't get to do anything. For a lot of people it probably isn't enough. Occasionally, you might find a big story dungeon with some unique enemies and blueprints. Those parts can be quite fun. But after you clear them out, you're back to the endless expanse of sea.

Furthermore, there is a lack of quality all throughout this game. When I can be sitting there, not moving nor interacting with anything, and then the shark can just clip halfway through my raft, its not a great look. Not just the shark, but the other sea life (god forbid its the huge whale that will actually just steal you from your raft), or the flotsam that litters the sea. Even past the clipping issues, the game just has a B-tier feeling to it. All the animations feel pretty poor, and lack any sort of oomph to them. They're not really the highlight of the game for me.

With all this in mind, it sounds like my review doesn't have much to say. I have issues with both the major and minor details of this game, from the game design foundations to the extra polish. So why do I recommend Raft? One reason: this game allows you and your friends to undergo mass psychosis with ease. I am not sure I can truthfully describe this phenomenon that occurs when playing this game. It feels like you've been drained of all energy, starving and thirsting, on a deserted island, but with your friends. Every single time I tried playing this in recent memory, we devolve into dopey giggling about stupid shit we think of. It is the funniest shit ever and then I forget the next day because it all felt like a fever dream. Its not something that just any game can do. But Raft does it for some reason, and its really funny

A Series of Unfortunate Rafts

“Raft™ throws you and your friends into an epic oceanic adventure! Alone or together, players battle to survive a perilous voyage across a vast sea!”

--Gameplay: 7/10

What sets Raft apart from most other survival games is its approach to the base-building mechanic. As the name implies, your raft is your base. Not only that, but it also serves as your means of travel through the endless ocean. With this approach, the game essentially eliminates the backtracking that you would normally have to do after long trips in other games. 

Expanding your raft, upgrading it with proper navigation and engines, and watching it slowly become a proper self-sustaining vessel is a very rewarding experience. It is further reinforced by the many decoration options available to you, allowing you to fully customize it to your liking.

Combat, however, in this game is a different story. It is overly simple and easy, poses no real threat, and offers no challenge or player engagement. Enemies usually have one or two attacks that are easily avoided, often not requiring more than two steps to the side. Because of this, combat encounters become a nuisance very soon and are ultimately best avoided, especially since there are no worthwhile rewards.

Resource gathering can be quite a slow process, and paired with most crafting recipes requiring a high material cost, Raft can often feel grindy and slow, even with multiple players.

After finishing your daily errands and the maintenance required to keep your vessel operating, you might often find yourself stuck out in the ocean with nothing to do but wait. That is a drawback of having a floating base out in the ocean, since downtime becomes considerably more boring. You will sit and wait to reach the next island, wait for floating debris to drift your way so you can collect materials and build, or just wait for various production tasks to finish.

Exploration outside the story islands is sadly quite bland. Other than the story islands, the islands you find out in the world are all pre-built, with only a handful of variations, and are randomly placed throughout the ocean. Being pre-built means that very soon you will see all the island variations, and after a while, it just becomes a matter of going to the same islands over and over again.

--Story & World (No Spoilers): 6/10

What I appreciate about this game's story is that it keeps you in the dark, and it essentially feeds you breadcrumbs and guides you to the next destination to uncover secrets and more information about the world.

As mentioned before, the game has these story islands where you will find pieces of information about the world and its characters. These islands themselves are way more intriguing and fun to explore, diverse, and beautifully built. As you progress through the story, they become increasingly more detailed and complex, with more interesting island designs, puzzles, and obstacles to overcome.

The story itself is nothing overly amazing. It is a simple story more focused on characters, and it gets the job done in order to give you some purpose and a reason to explore and move on further.

--Graphics & Art Style: 7/10

The game has this low-poly art style that gives the game a colorful and slightly cartoonish vibe. It is not overly unique, as similar art styles can be seen in other games, but where it truly shines is in its attention to detail. Tools, contraptions, furniture, and all the other items you build and find have this very interesting and detailed makeshift aesthetic to them, making objects look like they were really built by collecting scraps and junk. The game's graphics shine especially well when you have a larger and more decorated base, where all these individual objects and decorations come together nicely.

The graphics fall off a bit when you find yourself on random islands, as they tend to have rather simple geometry and repetitive design choices, with very little variation and a lack of unique details.

One thing that I believe is a miss in this department is the game's weather effects. For a game taking place 90% of the time on the ocean, I would have loved to see some proper thunderstorms, more violent waves that could impact your raft's navigation, or even hurricanes. This would have added another layer of immersion to the world and opened up additional gameplay options, like waves damaging your raft or impacting navigation.

--Sound & Music: 7/10

The soundtrack, I feel, does not have any overly iconic, memorable, or unique tracks, but what it does have is ambient music and sound effects that fit the game's design and gameplay very well. It does not particularly stand out, but it does its job well, fitting in with the game's overall approach.

Where I must give my compliments is to the voice acting. I believe that most of the voice actors have done a wonderful job and conveyed the characters' personalities very well with the few voice lines they have. There are some minor, awkward-sounding lines, which I believe are mainly present because of the various accents that the actors have, but nothing immersion-breaking or difficult to listen to.

--Overall: 7/10

Raft is a solid survival game which will provide you with many hours of entertainment. However, with its gameplay, mainly the combat and high level of grind, this game is not for everyone. I believe it is more aimed towards people who want a more relaxed and casual approach to gaming where they can kick back and take their time, rather than players who seek action, thrills, or a challenge.

It balances all of its aspects very well, and some of the more negative points usually only become apparent later on in the game. Overall, I give it a 7/10: a decent game which is worth its price tag. Still, if you are unsure, maybe wait for a sale.

Here's a game where you start with almost nothing, floating in the middle of the ocean on a tiny raft, and slowly turn that little platform into a home. You gather materials, craft equipment, explore islands and reefs, research new technology, grow food, and try to keep everyone alive while a shark occasionally decides to take a bite out of your raft. LOL The best part for me is that you're figuring this all out together, so even the smallest problems can turn into  some of the funniest memories. At first, everyone is figuring out what they're supposed to be doing then it becomes a battle of resourcefulness and who gets to drink the boiled water first before you pass out from dehydration. But bob decides to say who cares and drinks the salt water instead. You learn who you can rely on, who is going to remember to gather something important, who picks the flowers, and who is absolutely going to swim off toward an island without telling anyone. You are forced to think about what you're using and what you're going to need later. It also makes  crafting feel rewarding because you can see the difference between having almost nothing and gradually having the equipment you need to survive. Crop plots were probably my least favorite task of the game, but I was fine because some of my friends genuinely enjoyed taking care of them. I loved building the raft the most. The research table is another system I really liked. Instead of simply handing you every crafting recipe from the beginning, the game encourages you to discover materials and use them to learn what you can make. You gradually build up your knowledge and unlock better equipment. I think that it is a particularly good way to introduce someone to a survival game progression because it teaches you to experiment. If you don't know what something does, you find it, research it, and figure out how it can help you. I'd love to see this idea of discovery even further. More meaningful decisions, less simply following the next objective.
